append_only_log.name: Append-Only Log

verify: Why is an append-only log the fundamental data structure for a message queue? What properties does it give you?
How does sequential disk I/O make append-only logs performant? What throughput can you achieve?
deepen: Sequential writes to disk can achieve 600MB/s on a modern SSD. Random writes get maybe 100MB/s. How does your log structure exploit this?
Your log is append-only and immutable. How do you handle message deletion? You can't remove a message from the middle of the log.
challenge: A B-tree based database also provides ordered writes. Why not use a regular database as the message store instead of a raw append-only log?
anti_bs: You said 'write messages to a log.' What's the on-disk format? How are messages serialized? What metadata is stored alongside each message — offset, timestamp, key, headers?

common_mistakes: Not leveraging sequential I/O for performance
Trying to support random deletes in an append-only log
Not understanding why append-only outperforms random writes

topic_partition.name: Topics and Partitions

verify: What is the relationship between topics and partitions? Why do you need partitions?
How do you decide the number of partitions for a topic?
deepen: A topic has 12 partitions. Messages with key 'user-123' always go to partition 7 (hash-based). But partition 7 gets 10x more traffic than others because of a hot key. How do you handle this?
You have 12 partitions and ordering is guaranteed within a partition. But your consumer needs global ordering across all partitions. How do you achieve this?
challenge: You created a topic with 6 partitions. Traffic grew 10x and you need 60 partitions. But increasing partitions breaks key-based ordering guarantees. How do you handle this migration?
anti_bs: You said 'partition the topic.' By what key? How does the partitioner work — hash mod N, range-based, or custom? What happens when a message has no key?

common_mistakes: Too few partitions limiting parallelism
Too many partitions increasing metadata overhead
Not considering hot partition problem

producer_acks.name: Producer Acknowledgments

verify: What acknowledgment modes does your message queue support? What are the trade-offs between acks=0, acks=1, and acks=all?
When does the producer consider a message 'successfully sent'?
deepen: With acks=all, the producer waits for all in-sync replicas to acknowledge. If one replica is slow, it blocks the producer. How do you handle a slow replica without sacrificing durability?
acks=1 means only the leader acknowledges. If the leader crashes right after acknowledging but before replicating, the message is lost. When is this acceptable?
challenge: A financial system requires zero message loss (acks=all) but also needs sub-10ms latency. These goals conflict. How do you satisfy both?
anti_bs: You said 'the producer sends messages.' Does it wait for acknowledgment? From whom — the broker, the leader, all replicas? What happens on timeout?

common_mistakes: Using acks=0 or acks=1 for critical data without understanding the risk
Not handling producer timeouts
Not configuring min.insync.replicas with acks=all

consumer_groups.name: Consumer Groups

verify: What is a consumer group? How does it enable parallel consumption?
What's the relationship between the number of partitions and the number of consumers in a group?
deepen: A topic has 12 partitions and a consumer group has 15 consumers. What happens to the 3 extra consumers?
Two consumer groups subscribe to the same topic — Group A for real-time processing, Group B for analytics. How does the message queue deliver messages to both groups independently?
challenge: A consumer in the group is slow — it takes 10 seconds to process each message while others take 100ms. This consumer falls behind. How do you detect and handle this?
anti_bs: You said 'use consumer groups for scaling.' How are partitions assigned to consumers? What algorithm — range, round-robin, or sticky? What happens when a consumer joins or leaves?

common_mistakes: More consumers than partitions leaving consumers idle
Not understanding that partition is the unit of parallelism
Not monitoring consumer lag

offset_management.name: Offset Management

verify: What is a consumer offset? How does the consumer track which messages it has processed?
What's the difference between auto-commit and manual offset commit?
deepen: Auto-commit commits offsets every 5 seconds. If the consumer crashes 3 seconds after the last commit, it reprocesses 3 seconds of messages on restart. How do you handle this?
A consumer commits offset 1000 but crashes before processing messages 998-1000. On restart, it starts from 1001 — messages 998-1000 are lost. How do you prevent this?
challenge: Manual commit after processing each message is safest but adds latency. Auto-commit is fast but risks reprocessing or loss. Is there a middle ground?
anti_bs: You said 'track offsets.' Where are they stored — in the message queue itself, in ZooKeeper, or in an external database? What's the commit frequency?

common_mistakes: Committing offset before processing (risking message loss)
Auto-commit causing duplicate processing after crash
Not understanding at-least-once vs at-most-once semantics

isr_replication.name: In-Sync Replica (ISR) Replication

verify: What is an in-sync replica (ISR)? How does it differ from a regular replica?
What is the high watermark and how does it relate to consumer visibility?
deepen: A replica falls behind the leader by 10 seconds due to network issues. It gets removed from the ISR. What happens to acks=all producers? What if min.insync.replicas is 2 and only 1 replica remains in ISR?
The leader has messages up to offset 1000. Replica A has up to 995, Replica B up to 998. The high watermark is 995. A consumer can only read up to 995. Why is this important?
challenge: Synchronous replication (acks=all) ensures durability but limits throughput to the speed of the slowest ISR member. How do you balance durability vs. throughput?
anti_bs: You said 'replicate for durability.' How many replicas? Synchronous or asynchronous? What's the ISR threshold for removing a lagging replica?

common_mistakes: Not configuring min.insync.replicas
Not understanding high watermark and consumer visibility
Not monitoring ISR shrinkage

leader_election.name: Leader Election

verify: Each partition has a leader that handles reads and writes. What happens when the leader broker crashes? How is a new leader elected?
Who triggers leader election — the brokers themselves, a controller node, or an external coordination service?
deepen: During leader election, the partition is unavailable for writes. How long does election typically take, and how does this affect producers?
Unclean leader election: the only available replica is out-of-sync (missing recent messages). Do you elect it as leader (accepting data loss) or keep the partition offline?
challenge: Your cluster has 100 brokers and one controller. The controller crashes. Now you need to elect a new controller AND re-elect leaders for all partitions that were on the crashed broker. How do you avoid a cascading failure?
anti_bs: You said 'elect a new leader.' Using what algorithm? How does the system detect that the old leader is dead? What's the detection timeout?

common_mistakes: Not configuring unclean leader election policy
Not understanding the impact of leader election on availability
Single controller as a point of failure

segment_files.name: Log Segment Files

verify: Why is the log divided into segment files instead of a single ever-growing file?
What triggers a segment roll — file size, time, or both?
deepen: Each segment has an associated index file mapping offsets to byte positions. How does a consumer seek to offset 5,000,000 efficiently? Walk me through the index lookup.
Zero-copy transfer: the broker sends data from disk to the network socket without copying through user space. How does sendfile() work, and why is it critical for throughput?
challenge: Your segment files are 1GB each and you have 10,000 partitions. That's 10,000 open file handles minimum. How does the OS handle this, and what limits might you hit?
anti_bs: You said 'store messages on disk.' In what format? How are segments organized? What's the segment size, and how do you look up a message by offset?

common_mistakes: Segment size too large causing slow recovery
Not understanding zero-copy and its performance impact
Not considering file descriptor limits

retention_policy.name: Retention Policy

verify: How long do you keep messages? What determines when messages are deleted?
What's the difference between time-based and size-based retention?
deepen: You set retention to 7 days, but a consumer group was offline for 8 days. They come back and their offset points to deleted data. How do you handle this?
A topic with 50 partitions and 7-day retention stores 500GB of data. Suddenly a producer starts sending 10x the normal volume. Your disk fills up before 7 days. What happens?
challenge: Some events (like financial transactions) must be retained for 7 years by regulation. But most events need only 3 days. How do you handle different retention requirements on the same cluster?
anti_bs: You said 'retain messages for N days.' What happens to the disk space? Is deletion immediate or lazy? How does the broker reclaim space — delete whole segments or individual messages?

common_mistakes: Not monitoring disk usage vs retention
Consumers losing data because retention expired before consumption
Not understanding that deletion happens at segment granularity

compaction.name: Log Compaction

verify: What is log compaction and how does it differ from time-based retention?
When would you use log compaction instead of regular retention?
deepen: Compaction keeps the latest value for each key. But during compaction, the broker reads and rewrites segments — that's heavy I/O. How do you prevent compaction from impacting live read/write performance?
A tombstone (null value) marks a key for deletion during compaction. But what if a consumer reads the tombstone and doesn't understand it? How do you handle the delete.retention.ms window?
challenge: Your changelog topic uses compaction. A bug in a producer writes garbage values for 10,000 keys. After compaction, the garbage is the 'latest' value and the good data is gone. How do you recover?
anti_bs: You said 'use log compaction.' For what use case? How does the compaction thread work? What's the compaction lag, and how much extra disk space do you need during compaction?

common_mistakes: Not understanding when compaction vs retention is appropriate
Not reserving disk space for compaction process
Not handling tombstones properly

exactly_once.name: Exactly-Once Semantics

verify: What are the three delivery semantics — at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once? How does your system achieve exactly-once?
Is true exactly-once delivery possible, or is it exactly-once processing? What's the difference?
deepen: Exactly-once in Kafka uses transactions: consume from topic A, process, produce to topic B, commit offsets — all atomically. Walk me through how this works and what happens if the consumer crashes mid-transaction.

Exactly-once between your message queue and an external database requires two-phase commit or outbox pattern. The external system doesn't support transactions with your queue. How do you achieve end-to-end exactly-once?
challenge: A purist says 'exactly-once is impossible in a distributed system due to the Two Generals Problem.' How do you respond? What does 'exactly-once' really mean in practice?
anti_bs: You said 'guarantee exactly-once.' Between which components? End-to-end or just within the queue? What mechanisms make it work — transactions, idempotent producers, or both?

common_mistakes: Claiming end-to-end exactly-once without qualifying scope
Not understanding that exactly-once requires idempotent consumers or transactions
Confusing delivery guarantee with processing guarantee

idempotent_producer.name: Idempotent Producer

verify: What is an idempotent producer? How does it prevent duplicate messages on retry?
How does the broker detect that a retried message is a duplicate?
deepen: The broker assigns a Producer ID (PID) and tracks sequence numbers per partition. If the producer crashes and restarts, it gets a new PID. How does this affect exactly-once guarantees?
The broker keeps a window of recent sequence numbers for dedup. How large is this window? What happens if the producer skips a sequence number?
challenge: Idempotent producers prevent duplicates within a single producer session. But if two producers send the same logical message (e.g., same order event), the broker can't dedup across producers. How do you handle application-level dedup?
anti_bs: You said 'make the producer idempotent.' How? What protocol-level mechanism does the broker use to detect and discard duplicates?

common_mistakes: Thinking idempotent producer handles cross-session dedup
Not understanding PID and epoch semantics
Not enabling idempotency for critical producers

consumer_rebalancing.name: Consumer Rebalancing

verify: What triggers a consumer rebalance? What happens during a rebalance?
During a rebalance, is the consumer group still processing messages?
deepen: Eager rebalancing: all consumers stop, revoke all partitions, and reassign. This causes a 'stop-the-world' pause. How long does it last for a group with 100 consumers and 500 partitions?
Cooperative (incremental) rebalancing only moves affected partitions. How does it work, and why is it better than eager rebalancing?
challenge: A consumer is slow due to GC pauses and keeps triggering rebalances (heartbeat timeout). Each rebalance disrupts the entire group. How do you prevent one bad consumer from destabilizing the group?
anti_bs: You said 'the group rebalances.' What assignment strategy do you use? How do you minimize the number of partition movements during rebalance?

common_mistakes: Not understanding the impact of eager rebalancing
Not tuning heartbeat and session timeouts
Not using sticky or cooperative assignment strategy

backpressure.name: Backpressure Handling

verify: What happens when a consumer can't keep up with the production rate? How does your system handle backpressure?
Does your message queue apply backpressure on the producer, buffer in the broker, or let the consumer fall behind?
deepen: The producer sends 100K messages/sec. The consumer processes 10K messages/sec. After 1 hour, there are 324 million unconsumed messages. How much memory/disk does this consume, and what's the impact?
Producer-side backpressure: the broker rejects new messages when the queue is full. But the producer might lose important messages. How do you handle this without data loss?
challenge: In Kafka, consumers pull messages. There's no explicit backpressure — slow consumers just have increasing lag. In RabbitMQ, the broker pushes and can apply credit-based flow control. Which model is better and why?
anti_bs: You said 'handle backpressure.' How specifically? What's the buffer size limit? What happens when the buffer is full — block the producer, drop messages, or spill to disk?

common_mistakes: No monitoring for consumer lag
Unbounded buffers leading to OOM
Not distinguishing between pull-based and push-based backpressure models

capacity_estimation.name: Capacity Estimation

verify: How many messages per second does your message queue need to handle? What's the average message size?
Walk me through the math — messages/sec × message size × replication factor × retention period = total storage.
deepen: At 1 million messages/sec with 1KB average size, that's 1GB/sec of write throughput. With replication factor 3, it's 3GB/sec. How many brokers do you need if each broker handles 500MB/sec?
7-day retention at 1GB/sec ingest = 604 TB of raw data, times 3 replicas = 1.8 PB. How many disks do you need, and what's the cost?
challenge: Your capacity plan assumes steady-state throughput. But event-driven systems have bursts — a flash sale might produce 10x normal volume for 30 minutes. How do you size for bursts vs. average?
anti_bs: You said 'handle millions of messages.' Per second or per day? What's the message size? Show me the storage and network bandwidth calculation.

common_mistakes: Not accounting for replication in storage and bandwidth calculations
Not considering burst traffic
Forgetting network bandwidth as a bottleneck alongside disk
